question: What is the main difference between an antiseptic and a disinfectant?

options.A: Antiseptics are heated before use, while disinfectants are kept at room temperature.
options.B: Antiseptics are used on living tissue, while disinfectants are used on inanimate surfaces.
options.C: Disinfectants are safe to drink, while antiseptics are strictly for external wounds.
options.D: Disinfectants kill viruses, while antiseptics only kill bacteria and fungi.

explanation: Antiseptics are formulated to be safe enough for human skin and wounds, whereas disinfectants are harsh chemicals meant only for objects and furniture. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h1)

question: Why shouldn't you use a strong hospital surface disinfectant on an open wound?

options.A: It will cause severe chemical burns and damage the living tissue.
options.B: It will make the bacteria grow faster inside the wound.
options.C: It will change the color of the patient's skin permanently.
options.D: It will wash away the local anesthetic effects.

explanation: You got it! Disinfectants are way too strong for human cells. They would destroy healthy tissue along with the germs, causing serious injury.

question: What does alcohol do to a germ's proteins when you use it for cleaning?

options.A: They multiply rapidly to protect the cell.
options.B: They are denatured and lose their normal shape.
options.C: They dissolve completely into pure water.
options.D: They turn into hard crystals of calcium.

explanation: Brilliant! Alcohol messes up the structure of microbial proteins, making them unfold and clump together, which destroys the germ.

question: How do soaps and surfactants mainly destroy germs on the skin?

options.A: By freezing the internal water inside the cell
options.B: By blocking the cell from taking in sunlight
options.C: By turning the cell into pure oxygen gas
options.D: By disrupting and breaking down the outer cell membrane

explanation: Exactly! Surfactants attack the fatty outer layer of the germ's cell wall, causing it to burst open and spill its contents.

question: Which skin antiseptic keeps working for hours after you apply it?
explanation: Spot on! Chlorhexidine sticks to the skin and keeps killing bacteria long after you put it on, which is why we love it for surgical scrubs.

question: Why do we only use glutaraldehyde on medical equipment instead of human skin?

options.A: It turns the skin bright yellow for several weeks.
options.B: It is a high-level disinfectant that releases toxic fumes and irritates skin.
options.C: It instantly evaporates when it touches human skin.
options.D: It only works when it is mixed with hot boiling water.

explanation: That's right! Glutaraldehyde is extremely harsh and gives off strong fumes, so it belongs in soaking tanks for instruments, never on a patient's skin.

question: Why must you wash off blood and dirt before putting a disinfectant on a surface?

options.A: Organic matter shields the microorganisms and blocks the chemical from working.
options.B: Blood mixes with the disinfectant to create a pleasant scent.
options.C: Blood changes the color of the disinfectant so it looks clean.
options.D: Organic matter makes the disinfectant evaporate too slowly.

explanation: Correct! Blood and body fluids can hide germs and block the disinfectant from reaching them. Always clean first, then disinfect!

question: What does the term 'contact time' mean when using a disinfectant?

options.A: The number of hours the nurse wears gloves during the shift
options.B: The time the surface must stay wet with the product to kill germs
options.C: The time it takes for the liquid bottle to completely empty
options.D: The time it takes for the skin to dry after a scrub

explanation: Disinfectants do not work instantly; they require a specific duration of continuous wetness to fully eliminate pathogens. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h4)

question: When is traditional handwashing with soap and water required instead of an alcohol-based hand rub?

options.A: When the patient has a known allergy to clear water
options.B: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.C: Whenever the nurse enters a patient's private room
options.D: At the beginning and end of every single nursing shift

explanation: Alcohol rubs cannot remove heavy organic material or certain spore-forming germs, so visible dirt requires physical washing with soap and water. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h5)

question: How should you apply skin antiseptic before putting in an IV line?

options.A: Scrub back and forth rapidly over the exact insertion point only.
options.B: Apply the antiseptic and immediately wipe it dry with sterile gauze.
options.C: Start at the center of the site and wipe outward in concentric circles.
options.D: Pour the liquid directly into the vein before inserting the needle.

explanation: Brilliant! Moving from the clean center outwards pushes germs away from the spot where the needle will enter.

question: What major safety hazard is linked to alcohol-based skin preps in the operating room?

options.A: They explode if exposed to cold refrigerated temperatures.
options.B: They release toxic green gases that paralyze the respiratory tract.
options.C: They permanently stain the operating room floor dark purple.
options.D: They are highly flammable and can catch fire if not dried before using cautery.

explanation: That's right! Alcohol evaporates into flammable fumes. If it's still wet when the surgeon's electrical equipment sparks, it can catch fire.

question: Why are newborn babies and burn patients at higher risk of chemical absorption from skin antiseptics?

options.A: Their skin barrier is immature or damaged, allowing greater chemical absorption.
options.B: They are allergic to all known chemical disinfectants in the hospital.
options.C: Their body temperature causes the antiseptics to boil on contact.
options.D: They produce natural enzymes that turn antiseptics into dangerous poisons.

explanation: Spot on! Delicate baby skin or open burn wounds lack that tough outer layer that normally stops chemicals from sinking into the bloodstream.

question: What practice helps germs develop resistance to chemical disinfectants?

options.A: Allowing alcohol-based hand rubs to air-dry completely on the skin
options.B: Changing cleaning cloths and disinfecting solutions after every single room
options.C: Washing hands with soap and water after caring for every infectious patient
options.D: Using disinfectants at too weak a dilution or cutting down the required contact time

explanation: You nailed it! If a disinfectant is too weak or wiped away too early, the tougher germs survive and learn to resist the chemical over time.

question: Which of these should you NEVER do when handling hospital disinfectants?

options.A: Disposing of expired chemical solutions safely according to policy
options.B: Guessing the dilution ratio without reading the manufacturer instructions
options.C: Following hospital guidelines for surface cleaning and equipment processing
options.D: Respecting the exact contact time required for the specific product

explanation: Exactly! Never guess dilutions. If you mix chemicals too weak, they won't kill germs; too strong, and they can harm someone. Always check the label!
